checks.explanation: The enforcing DMARC policy p=reject requests that mail receivers reject messages outright when neither SPF nor DKIM passes with an aligned domain. Only one of SPF or DKIM needs to pass with alignment for the message to pass DMARC. DKIM is the more resilient mechanism because it survives mail forwarding.

tags.label: Version
tags.explanation: Valid DMARC version identifier. Required as the first tag.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Both RFC 7489 and RFC 9989 require v=DMARC1 to be the first tag. A record with it anywhere else is not a DMARC record.

tags.label: Policy
tags.explanation: Strongest enforcement. Direct spoofing of this domain is blocked at receivers that apply DMARC.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies policy semantics and removes ambiguities in how receivers interpret these values. The biggest change is replacing pct with the binary t=y test mode for safer policy rollout.

tags.label: Subdomain Policy
tags.explanation: Subdomains inherit the root policy (p=reject). Setting sp= explicitly makes the record say what it means, so a later change to p= cannot loosen subdomains by accident.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies inheritance. sp covers subdomains that have no DMARC record of their own; np, imported from RFC 9091, lets non-existent subdomains carry a stricter policy than real ones.

tags.label: Non-Existent Subdomain Policy
tags.explanation: No non-existent subdomain policy. Falls back to sp= (if set), then p=. Current effective policy for non-existent subdomains: p=reject.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 brings np in from RFC 9091. Under RFC 7489 a subdomain that does not exist inherited sp, or p when sp was absent, so it could not be set separately. np lets you hold sp=none while a real subdomain is still being aligned and reject mail from names that were never created at the same time.

tags.label: DKIM Alignment Mode
tags.explanation: Defaults to relaxed (r). Subdomain alignment is permitted.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies alignment edge cases, especially around subdomains and how organizational domain is determined (now via tree walk instead of PSL).

tags.label: SPF Alignment Mode
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 explicitly states that DMARC evaluates SPF against the MAIL FROM identity only, not HELO. RFC 7489 let receivers fall back to HELO when MAIL FROM was empty.

tags.label: Failure Reporting Options
tags.explanation: Defaults to fo=0. Reports only on complete failure of both mechanisms.
tags.dmarcbis_note: The fo tag is defined in RFC 9989 section 4.7, but the reports it governs are specified in RFC 9991. Most large receivers, Google and Microsoft among them, do not send failure reports at all.

tags.label: Aggregate Report Recipients
tags.explanation: Aggregate reports are sent to mailto:d@rua.agari.com,mailto:dmarc_agg@vali.email. These show which sources send mail as your domain and whether they pass or fail authentication. These reports are how you find legitimate senders failing authentication before their mail is rejected.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Reporting moved into its own documents: RFC 9990 for aggregate reports and RFC 9991 for failure reports. The size suffix on a URI (such as !10m) was removed (RFC 9989 Appendix C.4). URI syntax is otherwise unchanged.

tags.label: Forensic Report Recipients
tags.explanation: Failure reports sent to mailto:d@ruf.agari.com,mailto:MTc4Mzcw@ruf.vali.email. Most providers including Google and Microsoft do not send failure reports due to PII concerns.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Failure reporting is now defined in its own document, RFC 9991.

tags.label: Percentage
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Report Format
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Report Interval
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Public Suffix Domain
tags.explanation: Not declared, which is the RFC 9989 default ('u') and correct for almost every domain. Receivers determine the organizational domain with the tree walk. Publish psd= only if this domain is a public suffix.
tags.dmarcbis_note: New in RFC 9989. It replaces the Public Suffix List, a file maintained outside DNS, for finding the organizational domain.

tags.label: Testing Mode
tags.explanation: Normal enforcement. Policies applied as published.
tags.dmarcbis_note: New in RFC 9989, replacing pct. Under RFC 7489, pct=50 meant 'apply to 50% of failing mail', but receivers implemented it inconsistently. Only pct=0 and pct=100 were reliable. t=y asks receivers to apply one level below the published policy. t=n, or no t tag, applies it in full.

config_warnings.title: Underutilized failure reporting
config_warnings.text: Failure reporting is configured but set to report only when both SPF and DKIM fail. You are missing most failure data. Set fo=1 to capture all failures.

config_warnings.title: Implicit subdomain policy
config_warnings.text: Subdomains inherit p=reject by default, which is correct. Setting sp=reject explicitly makes the record say what it means, so a later change to p= cannot loosen subdomains by accident.

config_warnings.title: No explicit np= policy
config_warnings.text: No explicit non-existent subdomain policy. np is optional: it falls back to p=reject, so non-existent subdomains already get reject.

config_warnings.title: SPF alignment under RFC 9989
config_warnings.text: Under RFC 9989, SPF alignment is evaluated against the MAIL FROM (envelope sender) identity only, not HELO.

config_warnings.title: Mailing list participation
config_warnings.text: p=reject can cause mail sent through mailing lists to be rejected: the list relays from its own servers, which breaks SPF alignment, and often edits the subject or footer, which breaks the DKIM signature. Lists that rewrite the From header avoid this. ARC (Authenticated Received Chain) helps, but not all receivers support it yet.

config_warnings.title: RFC 9989 reporting restructured
config_warnings.text: RFC 9989 splits the specification into three separate RFCs: core mechanism, aggregate reporting, and failure reporting.

config_warnings.title: External reporting destinations
config_warnings.text: Aggregate reports are sent to domains: rua.agari.com, vali.email.

sections.title: What is RFC 9989 (DMARCbis)?
sections.content: RFC 9989 is the DMARC standard. Published in May 2026 on the IETF Standards Track, it replaces RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, the documents that defined DMARC until then. It is still widely called DMARCbis, the name it carried through the working group. It addresses real-world problems discovered over a decade of DMARC deployment: inconsistent parsing across receivers, unreliable percentage-based rollout, no protection for non-existent subdomains, and dependence on the manually-maintained Public Suffix List.

sections.title: What changed from RFC 7489?
items: Your record doesn't have an np= tag. np, brought into RFC 9989 from RFC 9091, sets a policy for subdomains that were never created. Under RFC 7489 they inherited sp, or p when sp was absent, so the two could not be set separately.
RFC 9989 defines the record grammar more strictly. A report address without mailto:, a duplicated tag, an empty value or a malformed URI that older tools accepted is now invalid.
RFC 9989 replaces the Public Suffix List with a DNS tree walk, capped at 8 queries, and adds the psd= tag so a domain can declare its own status.
RFC 9989 splits the specification into three separate RFCs: the core mechanism, aggregate reporting, and failure reporting.

sections.title: Where does this record stand?
sections.content: This scale reflects how completely the record matches RFC 9989, the current DMARC standard. Ready means it uses the current tags and needs no changes. Compatible means it works but leaves protection unused. Anything below that has gaps worth closing. This record is currently rated 'ready'.

sections.title: Why does this matter?
sections.content: When your domain can be spoofed, someone else can send phishing and fraud that appears to come from you. Your customers, partners, and employees see your name on it. The recipients who trusted it are harmed, and so is their trust in your real mail. RFC 9989 closes gaps RFC 7489 left open, particularly around non-existent subdomains and inconsistent receiver behavior.

sections.title: What should I do?
sections.content: See your personalized migration path above for step-by-step instructions to reach RFC 9989 Ready status.

checks.deliverability: Receivers are asked to reject mail that fails DMARC. Google, Yahoo, and Microsoft (Outlook.com) require a DMARC record from bulk senders; an enforcing policy also lets receivers act on mail that fails.

checks.explanation: Found 2 live DKIM public keys published in DNS. Sending providers detected: SendGrid. Each key is a TXT record at selector._domainkey.paypal.com. Receiving servers retrieve this key to verify the DKIM signature on incoming messages (RFC 6376). Note: this audit confirms the public key exists in DNS; it does not test live message signatures. Selectors were targeted using SPF-based sender discovery.

details.business_risk: This key is below the RSA size RFC 8301 recommends and should be rotated to a 2048-bit RSA key.

checks.fix: The following selectors use RSA keys below the recommended 2048 bits: s2 (1024-bit). Key rotation is provider-specific. Check your email provider's documentation for how to generate and publish a new 2048-bit RSA key pair.

keys.rating_label: Weak by modern standards. NIST deprecated 1024-bit RSA in 2013. Rotate to 2048-bit.

dkim_deep.rotation_guidance: Rotate s2 to 2048-bit. Steps: 1) Generate new key pair, 2) Publish new public key under new selector, 3) Configure mail server to sign with new selector, 4) After a few days, once mail signed with the old key has been delivered, empty its p= to revoke it.

checks.deliverability: This key (1024-bit) still verifies today. Rotate to 2048-bit before receivers stop accepting it.
checks.what_this_is: A signature added to every message you send, checked against a key you publish in DNS. It proves the message came from your domain and was not altered on the way.

checks.name: SPF
checks.record: v=spf1 include:pp._spf.paypal.com include:3ph1._spf.paypal.com include:3ph2._spf.paypal.com include:3ph3._spf.paypal.com include:3ph4._spf.paypal.com include:sendgrid.net include:aspmx.pardot.com ~all
checks.explanation: SPF record ends with ~all (softfail): servers not listed here are not authorized to send mail for this domain. The SPF result feeds DMARC, and the DMARC policy decides what happens to mail that fails. With DMARC in place, ~all and -all are both sound choices. Note: SPF uses 9 of the allowed 10 DNS lookups (RFC 7208 section 4.6.4). Approaching the limit. Plan for headroom before adding new services.

details.text: ~all (softfail): servers not listed are not authorized
You are using 9 of 10 allowed DNS lookups. Only 1 slot remains.

checks.fix: Monitor lookup count when adding new services.

spf_deep.all_explanation: Servers not listed are not authorized. Receivers treat a softfail as a signal and leave the outcome to DMARC.
optimizations: Your SPF record uses 9 of 10 allowed lookups. Audit your includes: remove services you no longer use and consolidate senders where possible.
spf_deep.dmarcbis_note: Under RFC 9989, SPF alignment is evaluated against the MAIL FROM (envelope sender) identity only, not HELO. SPF pass alone does not guarantee DMARC pass. The MAIL FROM domain must also align with the From header domain.

checks.deliverability: Your SPF record uses 9 of 10 allowed DNS lookups. You are close to the limit. Plan carefully before adding new sending services like Mailchimp, HubSpot, or SendGrid.
checks.what_this_is: A DNS record listing the servers allowed to send mail for your domain. A receiver compares the server that delivered a message against that list.

checks.name: MTA-STS
checks.explanation: While DMARC protects the identity of the sender, MTA-STS (RFC 8461) protects the connection. It prevents downgrade attacks where a network attacker forces email to be delivered without encryption. Without MTA-STS, a sending server that cannot reach your mail server over TLS falls back to plaintext and nothing tells you.
checks.fix: MTA-STS requires a DNS TXT record at _mta-sts.paypal.com and a policy file hosted at https://mta-sts.paypal.com/.well-known/mta-sts.txt. The policy file specifies your MX hosts and the TLS enforcement mode.
checks.deliverability: MTA-STS covers mail sent to you. It has no effect on how your outgoing mail is filtered.
checks.what_this_is: A policy you publish telling sending servers to require TLS when they deliver to you, and to give up rather than fall back to plaintext. Without it, an attacker on the network can strip the encryption and read the mail.

checks.name: TLS-RPT
checks.explanation: Without TLS-RPT (RFC 8460), you have no visibility into encryption failures on inbound email delivery. If a sending server cannot establish a secure connection with your mail server, it may fall back to plaintext delivery or fail silently. TLS-RPT provides daily reports on these failures, allowing you to identify certificate issues or misconfigurations before they affect delivery.
checks.fix: Publish a TLS-RPT TXT record at _smtp._tls.paypal.com. Requires a reporting address (rua=) that can receive JSON-formatted TLS failure reports: either your own mailbox or a reporting service.
checks.what_this_is: An address you publish so senders can report failed TLS connections to your mail servers. It is how you find out that delivery is being downgraded or blocked.

checks.name: BIMI
checks.explanation: BIMI record is published. BIMI is a brand recognition feature, not a security protocol. Your brand logo URL is configured. A certificate (VMC or CMC) is referenced in the a= tag.

details.text: The SVG declares the correct profile for BIMI.
The root svg element has no fixed width and height. Gmail expects fixed pixel values (for example width='96' height='96'), so the logo may not display even though the SVG is valid.

checks.fix: Set fixed pixel dimensions on the root <svg> element, for example width="96" height="96".
checks.what_this_is: Shows your logo beside your mail in the clients that support it. It is branding, not security, and it requires DMARC at quarantine or reject first.

checks.name: DNSSEC
checks.explanation: DNSSEC is enabled. Your DNS records are cryptographically signed per RFC 4033/4034/4035, allowing validating resolvers to confirm that responses have not been tampered with. This prevents cache poisoning and DNS spoofing, and is required for DANE to function.

details.text: DS record present at parent (chain of trust anchored)
DS digest matches DNSKEY (chain of trust verified)

checks.what_this_is: Signs your DNS records so a resolver can tell the answer it got is the answer you published. It stops an attacker from forging DNS answers for your domain, and it is what DANE is built on.

checks.name: CAA
checks.explanation: CAA records (RFC 8659) restrict which Certificate Authorities may issue TLS certificates for your domain. Compliant CAs check these records before issuance and must not issue if they are not listed. Certificate Transparency logs can be used to detect issuance by CAs not authorized in your CAA records.

details.text: CAA controls regular certificate issuance but does not separately restrict wildcard certificates. Wildcard issuance falls back to the issue tag. Adding issuewild gives you explicit control over wildcard certificates.
Without an iodef record, you will not be notified if a Certificate Authority receives a certificate request that violates your CAA policy.

checks.what_this_is: A DNS record naming which certificate authorities may issue certificates for your domain. It does not affect mail; it limits who can get a certificate in your name.

checks.name: Nameservers
checks.explanation: Found 4 nameservers for this domain. Nameservers are authoritative for your DNS zone. They answer queries for all your DNS records. Multiple nameservers on distinct network paths reduce the risk of a single point of failure causing a full DNS outage for your domain.

details.text: This audit does not check blocklist listings. Blocklist operators refuse queries from cloud-hosted resolvers, so the answer would not be reliable. Check yours at check.spamhaus.org
All nameservers are hosted by UltraDNS/Neustar. While this provider likely has internal redundancy, using a secondary DNS provider eliminates the risk of a provider-wide outage affecting your domain.

checks.what_this_is: The servers that answer every DNS question about your domain, including the records on this page. If they disagree with each other or stop answering, your mail and your website stop resolving.

checks.name: DANE
checks.explanation: DANE (RFC 7672) uses TLSA records to let sending mail servers verify your mail server's TLS certificate through DNS, without depending on the CA infrastructure. DANE requires DNSSEC to be effective. Without it, TLSA records cannot be trusted. DANE and MTA-STS serve complementary roles for enforcing SMTP TLS.

details.text: Checked 2 MX hosts, but no TLSA records found
DNSSEC is enabled and ready for DANE deployment

checks.fix:
DANE implementation requires multiple steps:
1. DNSSEC must be enabled and validated for your domain.
2. Generate a TLSA record containing the SHA-256 hash of your mail server's TLS certificate (SPKI). The record goes at _25._tcp.<mx-host>.
3. TLSA records must be updated every time you rotate your mail server's TLS certificate, or use DANE-TA (usage 2) to pin the CA certificate instead.
checks.what_this_is: Publishes your mail server's certificate fingerprint in DNSSEC-signed DNS, so a sending server can verify the certificate without trusting a certificate authority. It requires DNSSEC on your zone and it fails closed, so mail stops if the record and the certificate drift apart.

checks.name: Certificate Transparency
checks.explanation: Certificate Transparency was not assessed. This audit reads CT data from the public crt.sh service, which did not answer within five seconds. That is common for domains with thousands of certificates and says nothing about your certificates either way. To review them yourself, search this domain on crt.sh.

details.text: crt.sh did not answer in time. This is a gap in the audit, not a finding about your domain.

checks.what_this_is: Public logs that every certificate authority writes to when it issues a certificate. Reading them shows every certificate that exists for your domain, including ones nobody at your company ordered.

anomalies.title: Mixed DKIM key strengths
anomalies.description: Some DKIM selectors use 2048-bit (or larger) keys while others use 1024-bit keys. Weak selectors undermine the security of your DKIM setup.
anomalies.recommendation: Rotate all DKIM keys to 2048-bit RSA (or Ed25519) and retire any selectors with keys smaller than 2048 bits.

resilience.summary: SPF and DKIM both provide independent paths to DMARC alignment, and DMARC is enforcing. This is the strongest configuration. If one mechanism fails for a given message, the other can still satisfy DMARC on its own.

spf.note: SPF record is valid (9/10 lookups used). SPF verifies that the sending server's IP address is authorized by the domain owner. However, SPF breaks when mail is forwarded because the forwarding server's IP is not in the original domain's SPF record.

dkim.note: 2 DKIM selectors detected across multiple services. DKIM signs each message with a cryptographic signature that travels with the email. Unlike SPF, DKIM survives forwarding because the signature is attached to the message itself, not tied to the sending server's IP. Selectors found: s1, s2.

dmarc.note: DMARC policy is p=reject, the strongest enforcement level. Messages that fail both SPF and DKIM alignment will be rejected. Spoofed mail from this domain should not reach inboxes.

resilience.risk: The current policy is p=reject, the strongest enforcement level. Messages that fail both SPF and DKIM alignment are rejected outright. Having both mechanisms active matters because SPF and DKIM fail in different scenarios. SPF checks the sending server's IP against the domain's authorized list, which means it breaks when mail is forwarded through mailing lists, forwarding rules, or relay services. DKIM attaches a cryptographic signature to the message itself, so it survives forwarding. Of the two, DKIM is the more reliable alignment mechanism for this reason. DMARC requires identifier alignment: the domain authenticated by SPF or DKIM must match the domain in the visible From address. For SPF, the Return-Path domain must align with the From domain. For DKIM, the d= domain in the signature must align with the From domain. In relaxed mode (the default), subdomains of the same organizational domain satisfy alignment (e.g. mail.example.com aligns with example.com).

items.action: Rotate the weak DKIM key to 2048-bit
items.impact: This key is below current recommendations and should be rotated.
One more include, a, or mx mechanism would take this past 10. Past 10, receivers return PermError, none of the mail passes SPF, and DMARC relies on DKIM alone.
Without MTA-STS, a sending server that cannot reach your mail server over TLS falls back to plaintext and nothing tells you.
You get no report when a sending server fails to reach your mail server over TLS.
Without DANE, a sending server has no way to check your mail server's certificate against DNS; it trusts whichever certificate authority issued it.

items.impact: Purely optional. Subdomains already inherit your enforcing policy without it.
